reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders of bile formation presenting with chronic intrahepatic cholestasis, usually beginning in infancy or early childhood
Severe, often disabling pruritus and jaundice with progression toward cirrhosis is the typical course
Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase helps subtype the disease: it is characteristically low or normal in the ATP8B1 (PFIC1) and ABCB11 (PFIC2) forms but elevated in the ABCB4 (PFIC3) form
PFIC2, caused by defective bile salt export pump (ABCB11), carries an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma early in life
PFIC1 (ATP8B1) is associated with extrahepatic features such as diarrhoea, pancreatitis, and hearing loss because the defect is not confined to the liver
PFIC3 reflects impaired phospholipid transport across the canalicular membrane, leading to bile that damages the biliary epithelium
Fat malabsorption with failure to thrive and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency requires nutritional support

Options include measures to interrupt bile acid enterohepatic circulation, biliary diversion surgery, and liver transplantation for end-stage disease, with newer bile acid transport inhibitors used for pruritus
reference.pathophysiology: PFIC comprises inherited defects in the proteins that generate and secrete bile at the hepatocyte canalicular membrane. In the ATP8B1-related form (PFIC1) a defective aminophospholipid flippase destabilises the canalicular membrane and impairs bile secretion, with effects in other epithelia. In the ABCB11-related form (PFIC2) the bile salt export pump fails, causing intracellular accumulation of toxic bile acids and hepatocyte injury. In the ABCB4-related form (PFIC3) deficient phospholipid translocation leaves bile depleted of protective phospholipid, so unbuffered bile acids injure the bile ducts and produce a high-GGT cholestasis. Additional subtypes involve tight-junction and other transport proteins. Retained bile acids drive pruritus, progressive fibrosis, and eventual cirrhosis, while reduced intestinal bile delivery causes fat and vitamin malabsorption.
additionalInvestigations: Serum GGT level to help discriminate transporter subtypes
Genetic testing for ATP8B1, ABCB11, ABCB4, and other implicated genes
Serum and urinary bile acid profiling to exclude synthesis defects
Liver biopsy with immunostaining for canalicular transport proteins
Assessment of fat-soluble vitamin status and growth
Surveillance imaging and alpha-fetoprotein for hepatocellular carcinoma in high-risk subtypes
redFlags: Progression to cirrhosis with hepatic decompensation
Development of hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly in the bile salt export pump defect
Intractable pruritus severely impairing quality of life
Bleeding due to vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease tends to progress to cirrhosis and liver failure during childhood; biliary diversion and pharmacological interruption of bile acid recycling can improve symptoms and slow progression in some subtypes, while liver transplantation is often required for end-stage disease, and there is a subtype-specific risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
pitfalls: Ignoring the diagnostic value of the GGT level when subtyping cholestasis
Missing hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in the ABCB11 (PFIC2) form
Overlooking extrahepatic manifestations in the ATP8B1 (PFIC1) form
Failing to correct fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and support nutrition
